title: Retrieval Practice and where real evidence about learning comes from. Unfortunately.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Prompted by an issue of The Learning Dispatch, Skelton reads retrieval practice through his own idea of repeated experiences: each effort to pull something from memory strengthens neural pathways and helps learning stick. He argues that school structures with short, fragmented timetable periods crowd out retrieval and produce coverage rather than learning, and he contrasts this with the multi-week subject blocks of the International Primary Curriculum. He then takes up Carl Hendrick's caution that most testing-effect research comes from laboratories and university students rather than real classrooms. From that he draws a broader complaint that very little learning research is done in authentic schools, and in his whole career he can recall no school hosting external classroom researchers. He closes by presenting colleague-to-colleague Looking for Learning visits as site-specific, classroom-based evidence that schools can gather for themselves.
points: Retrieval practice works because it is a form of repeated experience that demands an active brain, and the evidence suggests its presence matters more than how surrounding activities are ordered.
Fragmented timetables work against retrieval, whereas extended subject blocks give time for frequent recall and for skills to develop.
Most testing-effect evidence comes from laboratories and students unlike school pupils, so the step from lab finding to classroom practice is a translation that loses something.
Skelton argues that schools should build their own local evidence base about what helps learning in their own classrooms, and positions peer observation as a way to do so.
quotes: Retrieval Practice is a way of reinforcing learning by regular and frequent efforts to recall from memory - from the brain - what something is or how something is done. Retrieval practice is a different approach from passively reviewing or revising work on your own. At its heart, it is about repeatedly trying to get things from the brain.

Each repeated request to draw knowledge or skills from the brain creates a repeated experience that will, providing the practice is structured well, ensure that the neuronal pathways are reinforced a little at a time, enabling learning to become sticky.

Of course, the structures and systems of a school can get in the way of Retrieval Practice. If a school day or week is divided into short time periods, the lack of time available for retrieval practice is one of the reasons why we get coverage but not learning.

The stretched blocks enabled the young brains of primary/elementary children to stay focused for longer on science. They gave teachers more time to enable the skills of science to be learned. And, of course, they gave much more time each week for retrieval practice to happen quickly and often.

Very little evidence actually comes from research in real classrooms. There are reasons for this which are understandable. Classrooms and schools are messy places with multiple, often uncontrollable, variables. Research is difficult.

In all my time as a teacher, a Head of schools and someone who worked in hundreds of schools around the world, I can’t think of one occasion when a school with which I was involved was engaged with external researchers involved in classroom based research.

There is a reason why I know that retrieval practice is likely to work with more children, students and teachers than not. It is not because I have been involved in any number of controlled experiments with a highly selective control group. It is because I have spent hundreds of hours in the messiness of real classrooms looking at what enables learning to happen well and what enables it to happen badly.
